title: MCP_INIT_TIMEOUT=10s is tight for a cold remote initialize (TLS + DNS + server cold-start lands entirely inside this window)
description: For the remote_http transport, entering the streams context (line 118) is cheap — streamablehttp_client does not open a connection until the first POST. The first network round trip (DNS, TLS handshake, and the initialize POST to https://mcp.notion.com/mcp) therefore happens entirely inside `with anyio.fail_after(MCP_INIT_TIMEOUT): await session.initialize()` (lines 133-134) with MCP_INIT_TIMEOUT=10 (line 16). The underlying httpx client allows 30s, but the app caps it at 10s. A cold connection to a remote MCP server (first-hit TLS, server cold-start) can exceed 10s and will be hard-failed.
evidence:
line 16: `MCP_INIT_TIMEOUT = 10`
line 118: `transport_result = await exit_stack.enter_async_context(streams_context)`
line 133-134: `with anyio.fail_after(MCP_INIT_TIMEOUT):\n                    await session.initialize()`
impact: Cold connects to Notion's hosted MCP (or any remote server with slow cold-start) can spuriously time out at 10s and surface as a connection failure, even though the server would have answered within the SDK's own 30s budget. There is no retry around connect, so a single slow cold start fails the whole tool load.
suggested_fix: Raise MCP_INIT_TIMEOUT for remote transports (e.g. 30s to match the httpx default) or make it configurable, and/or add one retry on connect timeout.
verdict_reason:
All quoted evidence exists verbatim and the mechanism is code-proven. In /home/tennisbowling/open-webui/backend/open_webui/utils/mcp/client.py: line 16 `MCP_INIT_TIMEOUT = 10`; line 99 `transport_type = transport or "remote_http"` and line 114 `streams_context = streamablehttp_client(url, headers=headers)` (the default/remote branch); line 118 `transport_result = await exit_stack.enter_async_context(streams_context)`; lines 133-134 `with anyio.fail_after(MCP_INIT_TIMEOUT):\n    await session.initialize()`.

The finder's key premise — that entering the streams context is cheap and the first network round trip happens inside fail_after — is confirmed by the SDK at venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/mcp/client/streamable_http.py. The `streamablehttp_client` async CM (lines 478-510) only: creates a lazy httpx.AsyncClient via `create_mcp_http_client` (shared/_httpx_utils.py: just `httpx.AsyncClient(...)`, no connection), creates two in-memory streams (lines 475-476), starts the `post_writer` background task (line 491), and immediately `yield`s (line 502). No DNS/TLS/HTTP occurs on enter. The actual first POST is issued by `_handle_post_request` (line 260 `ctx.client.stream("POST", ...)`) which only runs when `session.initialize()` writes the initialize request into the write_stream — i.e. entirely inside the `anyio.fail_after(10)` scope. anyio.fail_after raises TimeoutError by cancelling the scope at the 10s deadline (confirmed from anyio source), a hard fail.

The app caps this at 10s while the SDK's own budget is `httpx.Timeout(transport.timeout=30, read=300)` (SDK __init__ default timeout=30 line 81; streamablehttp_client default timeout=30 line 448; open-webui passes no timeout override at client.py:114, so 30s applies). So a cold connect that the SDK would tolerate up to 30s is hard-failed at 10s.

No retry exists: the middleware tool-load caller (utils/middleware.py lines 2331-2410) catches the exception, disconnects the leaked client, appends to `mcp_failures` with `reason=f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"`, and `continue`s. A single slow cold start (e.g. Notion's hosted MCP, first-hit TLS + server cold-start) therefore drops that server's entire tool catalog. Bug is real.

title: disconnect() is not time-bounded; the streamable-http session-termination DELETE can block the event loop up to httpx's 30s timeout
description: disconnect() calls `await stack.aclose()` with no anyio.fail_after wrapper (lines 258-260). Closing the streamable-http transport runs the SDK's terminate_session(), which issues `await client.delete(self.url, ...)` to end the MCP session (Mcp-Session-Id). Unlike list_tool_specs/call_tool (which are wrapped in anyio.fail_after(MCP_CALL_TIMEOUT)), the teardown DELETE is bounded only by httpx's client timeout (30s default). The SDK swallows DELETE exceptions, so it won't raise, but it can still await up to ~30s.
evidence: line 258-260: `try:\n            await stack.aclose()\n        finally:`  (no fail_after around aclose)
impact: If Notion is slow/unresponsive at session-DELETE time, disconnect() (invoked at the end of every turn in main.py:2229 and in routers/mcp.py:_list_specs finally) can block for up to the httpx timeout per client, stalling the single event loop and delaying turn completion / shutdown.
suggested_fix: Wrap stack.aclose() in an anyio.move_on_after/fail_after (a few seconds) so a hung remote DELETE can't block teardown, while preserving the existing uncancel protection.
verdict_reason:
The quoted evidence exists verbatim. client.py:258-260 is `try:\n    await stack.aclose()\nfinally:` with no anyio.fail_after wrapper, in direct contrast to the two MCP-call paths that ARE bounded: list_tool_specs (line 157 `with anyio.fail_after(MCP_CALL_TIMEOUT)`) and call_tool (line 194 same). disconnect() has only the asyncio uncancel/restore dance, no timeout guard.

The DELETE chain is real. connect() at client.py:114 calls `streamablehttp_client(url, headers=headers)` passing NO timeout arg, so the SDK default applies. In the installed SDK (mcp 1.27.2, venv/.../mcp/client/streamable_http.py), streamablehttp_client signature defaults `timeout=30` (line 448) and on context teardown its finally block runs `await transport.terminate_session(client)` (lines 507-509) whenever `transport.session_id and terminate_on_close`. terminate_session (lines 423-437) issues `await client.delete(self.url, headers=headers)` (line 430) and swallows exceptions (`except Exception as exc: logger.warning(...)` at 436-437), so it won't raise but it WILL await. The httpx client is built with `timeout=httpx.Timeout(transport.timeout, read=transport.sse_read_timeout)` (line 484) where transport.timeout is the 30s default, and create_mcp_http_client (_httpx_utils.py:69-73) honors that Timeout. So the session-ending DELETE's connect/write/pool phases are bounded only by httpx's 30s, not by any open-webui guard.

Callers verified: main.py:2229 runs a plain sequential `await client.disconnect()` over `metadata['mcp_clients']` at turn-end cleanup (no asyncio.gather, no fail_after, no executor offload — grep found none in 2195-2235), and routers/mcp.py:257 calls it in the _list_specs finally. Both await on the single event loop. So a slow/unresponsive remote_http MCP server (e.g. Notion) at session-DELETE time can stall the loop up to ~30s per client during disconnect.

Severity low is correct: the stall is bounded at httpx's 30s (not unbounded), occurs only on teardown, swallows its own errors, and the finder explicitly acknowledged the 30s cap. The bug (missing time-bound on disconnect relative to the wrapped call paths) is genuine and code-proven.

title: call_tool() returns only `content` and drops `structuredContent`, losing structured tool output (2025-06-18 / outputSchema results)
description: call_tool dumps the full CallToolResult but returns only `result_dict.get('content', ...)`. CallToolResult also carries `structuredContent` (and `meta`), which the 2025-06-18 spec adds for tools that declare an outputSchema — and list_tool_specs deliberately captures outputSchema (lines 168, 173-174), so the client knows such tools exist. The structured payload is silently discarded; only the human-readable `content` blocks are returned.
impact: For Notion (or any) tools that return machine-readable results via structuredContent, the model only sees the text rendering and loses the structured object the outputSchema describes, degrading tool-result fidelity.
suggested_fix: Include structuredContent (and optionally meta) in the returned dict when present, e.g. return both content and structuredContent so callers can use the structured result.

title: Runtime MCPClient.connect() does not SSRF-validate the target MCP URL (validation only exists on the OAuth-discovery path)
description: connect() connects to whatever `url` it is given with no host/scheme validation. validate_public_url / _host_is_private exist in utils/mcp/oauth.py and are applied during OAuth discovery (oauth.py:106,127) and at the discover endpoint (routers/mcp.py:167), but they are NOT applied to the actual runtime transport connect in client.py. A connection.url pointing at a private/reserved/link-local/metadata IP (e.g. 169.254.169.254) is connected to directly, with any configured Authorization header attached.
impact: SSRF surface against internal/cloud-metadata endpoints from the server, plus the risk of sending a bearer token to a non-public host. Severity is tempered because a personal MCP url is normally set by the same user; the spec nonetheless requires validating the MCP url itself since it can come from a malicious server's discovery metadata.
suggested_fix: Call validate_public_url(url, allow_localhost=<policy>) at the top of connect() for remote transports before creating the streams context, consistent with the discovery path.
verdict_reason:
The cited evidence exists verbatim. In backend/open_webui/utils/mcp/client.py, MCPClient.connect() lines 110-114 do:
`elif url:\n  if transport_type == "remote_sse":\n    streams_context = sse_client(url, headers=headers)\n  else:\n    streams_context = streamablehttp_client(url, headers=headers)` — `url` is used directly with no host/scheme validation, and `headers` (which carry the Authorization bearer, set in build_*_connect_kwargs / build_personal_mcp_connect_kwargs) are attached.

The SSRF guards `validate_public_url`/`_host_is_private` live only in utils/mcp/oauth.py (defined at oauth.py:75,83) and are invoked exclusively on OAuth/discovery HTTP paths: fetch_json (oauth.py:106), discover_from_challenge (oauth.py:127), and the /discover endpoint (routers/mcp.py:167). They are never called on the runtime transport connect.

All three runtime connect sites confirm the gap:
- routers/mcp.py:253 (`_list_specs` → verify/tools) calls `client.connect(**connect_kwargs)` where connect_kwargs = `await build_personal_mcp_connect_kwargs(...)`. That builder (connections.py:147-158) returns `{"url": connection.url, ...}` with no validation.
- utils/middleware.py:2337 (personal MCP runtime) — same builder, same unvalidated url.
- utils/middleware.py:2482-2489 (global MCP runtime) calls `build_mcp_connect_kwargs(...)` which (client.py:77-81) returns `{"url": connection.get("url","") or None, ...}` unvalidated.

The save path performs no SSRF check either: routers/mcp.py `_validate_form` (lines 79-105) validates transport/auth_type/permissions but never calls validate_public_url; models/mcp.py insert_new_connection / update_connection_by_id_and_user_id store `url` verbatim. A connection.url of http://169.254.169.254/... is therefore connected to directly with the configured Authorization header.

The finder's premise that the URL can originate from a malicious server's discovery metadata is also confirmed: frontend PersonalMCPConnections.svelte:115 does `if (res?.endpoint) url = res.endpoint;`, taking the server-controlled `endpoint` from the /discover document and using it as the saved connection url, which then flows unvalidated into connect().

Severity 'low' is correct: the connection is a per-user resource behind get_verified_user auth and the features.mcp_remote_custom permission, so it is normally self-set; the residual risk is the discovery-metadata redirection vector plus bearer-token leakage to a non-public host. Note the runtime path is not even gated by allow_localhost — it is unconditionally unvalidated — which if anything is slightly worse than the finder implied, but the limited attacker control keeps it at low.

title: Token resolution at connect time has no per-connection refresh serialization; concurrent refreshes can trigger Notion grant revocation
description: Every connect() resolves the bearer via build_personal_mcp_connect_kwargs -> resolve_personal_bearer_token. When the access token is near expiry it calls refresh_token() and then persists the rotated tokens (lines 116-126) with NO lock, no SELECT...FOR UPDATE, and no per-connection mutex (grep for Lock/for_update across connections.py/oauth.py/models/mcp.py returns nothing). Two concurrent turns/subagents/workers for the same Notion connection can both read the same refresh_token and both POST /token. Per the live-verified Notion behavior, reusing a rotated-away refresh token beyond the short grace window makes the server REVOKE THE ENTIRE GRANT.
evidence:
line 116-126: `refreshed = await refresh_token(oauth, ...)
    tokens = {**tokens, **refreshed, "expires_at": token_expires_at(refreshed)}
    oauth["tokens"] = tokens
    await MCPConnections.update_oauth_by_id_and_user_id(connection.id, connection.user_id, oauth)`  # no serialization
line 137 (build_personal_mcp_connect_kwargs): `bearer_token = await resolve_personal_bearer_token(connection)`
impact: Concurrent connects for the same Notion connection (multiple chat turns, multiple subagents, or multiple workers) racing a token refresh can present a rotated-away refresh token and cause Notion to revoke the whole grant, forcing the user to fully re-authenticate. invalid_grant is terminal.
suggested_fix: Serialize refresh per connection (async lock keyed by connection.id plus a DB row lock / SELECT...FOR UPDATE), re-read tokens inside the lock, persist the new refresh_token atomically before releasing, and have other waiters reuse the freshly persisted access token instead of refreshing again.
verdict_reason: The quoted code exists verbatim. connections.py:113-127 (resolve_personal_bearer_token): when `expires_at and expires_at > int(time.time()) + 300` is FALSE (token within 300s of expiry), it unconditionally calls `refreshed = await refresh_token(oauth, ...)`, builds new tokens, and persists via `await MCPConnections.update_oauth_by_id_and_user_id(connection.id, connection.user_id, oauth)`. build_personal_mcp_connect_kwargs:137 calls this on every connect. There is NO serialization: grep for lock/for_update/mutex/semaphore/advisory/inflight/cache across connections.py, oauth.py, client.py and models/mcp.py returns nothing (only an unrelated comment in client.py:137). The persistence path update_connection_by_id_and_user_id (models/mcp.py:251-273) is a plain `UPDATE ... WHERE id == :id AND user_id == :user_id` with last-write-wins — no version column, no `WHERE updated_at = expected`, no SELECT...FOR UPDATE. Concurrent connects for the same connection are a real, encouraged path, not a contrived edge case: subagent.py:96-98 and 2106 explicitly document that `subagent_launch` is a parallelizable tool fanned out via asyncio.gather, and each subagent re-enters the full pipeline (subagent.py:1825 process_chat_payload → get_tools → middleware.py:2332 build_personal_mcp_connect_kwargs), reading the connection fresh from DB at middleware.py:2316-2320 (get_connection_by_id_and_user_id include_secrets=True) so each branch decrypts the SAME refresh_token. The line-113 guard is a pure read-only comparison against an identical DB value for both readers, so two near-expiry concurrent branches both fall through to refresh_token() and both POST /token with the same rotated-away refresh token. refresh_token() (oauth.py:258-282) reads `refresh = tokens.get('refresh_token')` from the passed oauth dict with no coordination. No token cache or in-flight-refresh dedup exists anywhere. The race is fully code-proven. The only external dependency is Notion's documented refresh-token-rotation reuse-detection (grant revocation on reuse), which the finder asserts as live-verified — that is provider behavior, not in this repo, but it is standard OAuth 2.1 / RFC 9700 rotation behavior. High is the right severity: terminal grant revocation forcing full re-auth, triggered by a normal parallel-subagent pattern; not critical only because it requires the near-expiry timing window plus concurrency and the worst-case revocation is provider-dependent.
